name: Wendy Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I coach singers at an opera house, sing small roles, record pronunciation guides and teach four private students. My music master’s helps with languages, but the useful work is hearing when a singer has learned the syllables without understanding the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has to fit around that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I share school pickup for our two children. We have a mortgage and ten months of expenses saved; I earn well, though rehearsal nights still need careful planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the company that faster rehearsal schedules are helpful if singers still get paid preparation time. I would keep coaching and singing rather than reorganise a good season around a small tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The opera contract and private pupils are paying, and our ten-month reserve covers a cancelled week. There are several other companies nearby if a season changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I would keep paid coaching calls, small roles and four pupils. I use AI occasionally to draft a translation note, then check every word with a printed libretto, the opera text, before a singer sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture. It does not suggest a drop in my own work or our household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a fee ever been disputed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guest rehearsal ran late last year and the extra hour was missing from the first invoice. I would ask the manager for written overtime terms before the next guest week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to another coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell her to keep the marked score and the timesheet. A sung phrase is work even when the audience never hears the rehearsal.

I would seek **written overtime terms** before the next guest week.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** covers a cancelled opera week without putting the household mortgage payment at risk.
Paid **coaching and pupils** make current income feel secure.
do: Keep **paid coaching**, small roles and four pupils this term.
Request **written overtime terms** before the next guest week.
feel: I feel **calm** about secure current work and income.
S0.quote: A sung phrase is work even when the audience never hears the rehearsal.
fieldNote: Her **paid opera contract**, four pupils, ten-month reserve and several nearby companies support a calm response to small AI changes.
Existing **AI translation drafts** are checked against the printed opera text.

steps.text: Keep paid opera coaching, small roles and four pupils this term
Request written overtime terms before next guest week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our coaches’ union that generated pronunciation guides could help rehearsals but may erase recording fees. We should bargain for paid coaching and preparation hours before managers swap them for software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guides and music notes provide about a fifth of my own pay. If those commissions shrink, my pupils do not automatically grow, and I would need to adjust the mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would bring the guide invoices to the coaches’ union and ask for written paid preparation hours in the next agreement. In the first year I would attend the librarian’s paid lesson on a new pronunciation checker, then test it only on a guide I own with no singer names and approved in-house storage; I would listen against the score and stop if a syllable changes or the file leaves the library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the recording fees even with savings. A good contract can buy time, but it cannot make a missing commission reappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload a student’s voice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The singer’s voice and name stay in our school files. I would test only my own unlabelled guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for another company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if paid guide and coaching hours actually fall. I would apply for a posted paid vocal-coach seat if my master’s qualifies, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and pickup fits; I would stay until an offer is signed.

I would tell management **recording fees** are part of real work.
think: Generated **pronunciation guides** could remove a fifth of my pay.

do: Bring **guide invoices** to the union and seek written paid preparation hours next month.
Test the **pronunciation checker** after paid instruction and approved library storage on my nameless guide; listen against score, stop errors/leakage.
Apply for a **posted coach seat** if paid hours fall, only if qualified, written net after travel replaces losses and pickup fits.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a real slice of my income.

fieldNote: Her **union request** concerns paid preparation and recording time, not a ban on tools.
A **new checker test** needs paid instruction, approved local storage, her nameless guide and manual listening.

Keep paid opera coaching until suitable written offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the opera house that AGI by 2028 can make a translation or guide in seconds. We need a signed schedule of human coaching hours, not an invitation to wait backstage for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most guide fees to disappear in 2028 and some coached rehearsal hours to be shortened. Robots that can sing on stage arrive about three years later, around 2031. My pronunciation-guide recording fees could disappear before any stage robot sings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total the guide invoices and request signed paid coaching dates. In the first year after 2028, if paid coaching hours also fall, I would apply for a posted conservatory voice post only if my master’s qualifies, its written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and school pickup fits; I would keep current pupils and opera calls until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the loss, but the ten-month reserve and nearby posts give me a way to search. If the opera stopped most coaching outright, I would be alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new teaching licence first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted role requires it and the school funds the course or pays study time. I would not spend the household reserve on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the conservatory merely hints at a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the opera work. I need a real posting with written hours and a signed offer before leaving.

Keep **current pupils** and paid opera calls until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost fees, with savings and nearby posts for control.
S2.quote: My pronunciation-guide recording fees could disappear before any stage robot sings.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 guide losses** before stage robots around 2031.
The **voice move** needs actual coaching cuts, a qualified posted vacancy, written net pay, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Count guide invoices and request signed paid opera coaching dates now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the singers that five years until AGI by 2031 lets us test a paid language-and-song class. A free taster is useful once. A regular paid song class has to pay its teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guide income could end by 2031, but a group may replace some of it if families pay. Stage robots follow around 2034, so I would not count on every small role continuing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would offer a six-week beginner song class only if the opera school has a room after our pickup, ten people prepay enough for room hire, a paid accompanist and my teaching and preparation time. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat only with ten paid places still covering those costs and a room and pickup that work; I would keep private pupils if the class fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about guide income shrinking while we test the class. We can absorb a failed pilot, but savings do not replace a recurring recording fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only six people pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six fees do not cover the room or both teachers. I would refund them rather than turn the accompanist into a volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the loan keyboards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school technician must inspect each loan keyboard and cable before students use them. If there is no safe instrument, I would use the room’s checked piano or cancel that place.

I would refund **six people** if fees fail to cover costs.
think: A **ten-place class** could replace some guide fees only after room and teaching costs are paid.
do: Start a **six-week song class** only with ten fees covering room, both teachers and preparation after pickup; require inspected instruments.
Repeat the **paid class** after 2031 only while ten fees cover room, both teachers/preparation, safe instruments and pickup.
Keep **private pupils** and refund six deposits if fees fail.
feel: I feel **anxious** about guide fees shrinking while testing a paid class.
S3.quote: A regular paid song class has to pay its teachers.
fieldNote: The **class gate** includes ten prepayments for room, accompanist, her teaching and preparation, plus pickup.
The school must **inspect loan keyboards** or use a checked piano; unsafe places are cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the opera house that a decade until AGI by 2036 is time to put paid teaching on a steadier footing. We can prepare for changes to opera coaching without pretending every paid rehearsal is already lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guides may stop selling by 2036, and stage robots could pressure small roles around 2039. Ten months saved and several nearby companies give us a route, but the mortgage means I still want proof of pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would save ten percent of each extra paid guest-coaching fee after the mortgage, food and lesson travel, aiming for twelve months while leaving six untouched. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid opera work and pupils and apply for a posted lead voice-tutor job only if my master’s qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost guide and role fees and pickup fits; I would leave only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about a change that far away, not worried about missing next month’s payment. The longer runway lets me build a better teaching contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra guest fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would save nothing new from that source. I would not raid six months of household reserves to claim progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a title for less pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A lead title must come with posted hours and written take-home pay that works after travel.

S4.quote: We can prepare for changes to opera coaching without pretending every paid rehearsal is already lost.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide fees could vanish quickly and coaching hours might follow. Signed paid opera calls, a posted teaching vacancy with genuine net pay and pickup that works would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the accompanist in a new class. A song class has two paid teachers when the vocal coach and accompanist both teach.

headlineQuote: A song class has two paid teachers when the vocal coach and accompanist both teach.
portrait: At **43**, Wendy is an opera vocal coach with a music master’s, two children, a mortgage and ten months saved.
Her higher **musician pay** comes from coached rehearsals, small roles, pronunciation guides and four pupils.
She uses **AI occasionally** and tests a new checker only after paid training, storage approval and manual listening.
A **paid song class** needs ten prepayments covering room, accompanist, teaching, preparation, safe keyboards and pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase guide fees and reduce paid coaching before she replaces the income.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed opera calls**, a posted qualified voice role with written net pay and workable pickup would help Wendy.
